extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students learning introductory set theory / proofs / discrete mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: Definitions, theorems, examples and exercises about images/preimages of functions and set cardinality (bijections, countable vs uncountable, Cantor diagonal argument) intended to teach and test understanding and proof skills in an introductory set theory / discrete math course.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition 12.9 — Image of a subset
rubrics_metrics.description: If f : A → B and X ⊆ A, the image of X is the set f(X) = { f(x) : x ∈ X } ⊆ B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In words: f(X) is the set of all things in B that f sends elements of X to. Think of f(X) as a 'distorted copy' of X inside B. Example computations (see Example 12.13 and 12.14) illustrate how to compute f(X) for finite sets and intervals. Note carefully that X must be a subset (not an element).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition 12.9 — Preimage of a subset
rubrics_metrics.description: If f : A → B and Y ⊆ B, the preimage of Y is f^{-1}(Y) = { x ∈ A : f(x) ∈ Y } ⊆ A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In words: f^{-1}(Y) is the set of all things in A that f sends into Y. f^{-1}(Y) is defined even when f is not invertible (it is a set-of-elements-of-domain). Warning/caution from text: f^{-1}(4) (using 4 as an element) has no meaning unless you intend the preimage of the singleton {4} or f^{-1} as an inverse function exists; be precise (use subsets). Examples show computing preimages of singletons and intervals and noting empty preimages when nothing maps into Y.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution — Syntax and semantic distinction between f^{-1} as preimage vs inverse function
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a subtle difference between f^{-1}(Y) meaning preimage of a subset Y ⊆ B and f^{-1} as an inverse function (which exists only when f is bijective). Likewise distinguish f({s}) versus f(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text emphasizes: X and Y in f(X) and f^{-1}(Y) are subsets, not elements. Example: f^{-1}({4}) = {s,x,z} while f^{-1}(4) (interpreting 4 as argument to an inverse function) is meaningless if f has no inverse. Be careful in notation and in exercises/counterexamples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem 12.4 — Basic image/preimage set identities
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are standard distribution and containment relations; note which are equalities and which only give containment (item 1 and 6 are generally only '⊆'). Exercises ask students to prove the subset relations and produce counterexamples where equalities fail (e.g., show f(W ∩ X) = f(W) ∩ f(X) is false in general). Use these identities when manipulating images/preimages in proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion — Prove or provide counterexample style (images/preimages)
rubrics_metrics.description: Common exercise tasks: compute f(X) and f^{-1}(Y) for given f and sets; prove subset/equality relations from Theorem 12.4; prove X ⊆ f^{-1}(f(X)) and determine when equality holds; prove or give counterexample for f(f^{-1}(Y)) = Y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text assigns concrete problems (e.g., Exercises 1–4, 5–14) to test computational skill and understanding, and to practice constructing proofs and counterexamples. A typical rubric for answers: correct computation, clear set notation, justification for subset or equality claims, explicit counterexample when a statement is false.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition 13.1 — Equality of cardinalities via bijection
rubrics_metrics.description: Two sets A and B have the same cardinality, written |A| = |B|, if there exists a bijective function f : A → B. If no such bijection exists then |A| ≠ |B|.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies to finite and infinite sets. To show |A| = |B| produce an explicit bijection (a formula is preferred over a table when possible). The inverse of any bijection is a bijection, and compositions preserve bijectivity. Use bijections to 'match up' sets to show they have equal size.

rubrics_metrics.name: Example / Criterion — Use of explicit bijections to show equal cardinality
rubrics_metrics.description: When demonstrating two sets have equal cardinality present a bijection (example: f(n) = -n shows |{0,..,5}| = |{-5,..,0}|; geometric and algebraic bijections show |(0,∞)| = |(0,1)| and |R| = |(0,1)| by composition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe bijection with a formula (not a table) when possible; justify injectivity and surjectivity. Transitivity of equality of cardinalities allows chaining bijections: if |A| = |B| and |B| = |C| then |A| = |C|.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cantor diagonal argument (Theorem 13.2) — Nonexistence of surjection N → R
rubrics_metrics.description: There exists no bijection f : N → R; the diagonalization constructs a real number b whose nth decimal differs from the nth decimal of f(n), ensuring b is not in the image of f, so f is not surjective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method: write hypothetical list of reals f(1), f(2),... with infinite decimal expansions, choose b whose nth decimal differs from nth decimal of f(n) (e.g., set it to 0 if that digit isn't 0 and 1 if it is). Use this construction to produce b ∈ R not equal to any f(n). The diagonal method is a standard proof technique for uncountability and for proving |A| < |P(A)| later; ensure careful handling of decimal representation ambiguities when writing formal proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition 13.2 — Countably infinite vs uncountable
rubrics_metrics.description: A set A is countably infinite if |N| = |A| (there exists a bijection N → A). A is uncountable if A is infinite and |N| ≠ |A| (no bijection N → A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Countably infinite sets can be listed in an infinite sequence a1,a2,...; uncountable sets cannot. Reserve ℵ0 for the cardinality of the naturals. Use constructive listings or bijections to show countability; use diagonalization or other arguments to show uncountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition 13.3 — Symbol ℵ0
rubrics_metrics.description: The cardinality of the natural numbers is denoted ℵ0. Any countably infinite set has cardinality ℵ0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ℵ0 as notation when comparing sizes of infinite sets (e.g., ℵ0 < |R|).

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem 13.3 — Characterization of countably infinite sets
rubrics_metrics.description: A set A is countably infinite if and only if its elements can be arranged in an infinite list a1, a2, a3, ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To prove a set is countable, either produce a bijection N → A or give an explicit infinite listing. Conversely, a listing a_n defines a bijection f(n)=a_n. This theorem is used repeatedly in exercises and proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem 13.4 — Rationals are countable (constructive listing)
rubrics_metrics.description: The set Q of rational numbers is countably infinite; construct an infinite array of rationals and follow a 'snake' path that lists every rational (in reduced form) to produce a bijection N → Q.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constructive proof: arrange rationals in grid indexed by numerator and denominator, remove repeats by using reduced form, and traverse diagonally. Students should be able to produce such an ordering and justify that every rational appears exactly once on the path.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem 13.5 — Product of two countable sets is countable
rubrics_metrics.description: If A and B are both countably infinite, then A × B is countably infinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof via listing elements of A and B and following a path through the grid (diagonal or snake) to list all ordered pairs. Use this construction or give a bijection to N. This generalizes to finite Cartesian products (Corollary 13.1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary 13.1 — Finite product of countables is countable
rubrics_metrics.description: Given n countably infinite sets A1,...,An (n ≥ 2), their Cartesian product A1 × ... × An is countably infinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by induction using Theorem 13.5 and the standard bijection between (A1×...×Ak)×Ak+1 and A1×...×Ak+1. Students should be prepared to use induction and explicit bijections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem 13.6 — Union of two countable sets is countable
rubrics_metrics.description: If A and B are both countably infinite, then A ∪ B is countably infinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by 'shuffling' lists: interleave elements a1,b1,a2,b2,... (omitting duplicates). Exercises often ask to formalize this and to handle overlap carefully (do not list elements twice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem 13.7 — Cantor's Theorem (|A| < |P(A)|)
rubrics_metrics.description: For any set A, |A| < |P(A)|: there exists an injection A → P(A) (x ↦ {x}), but no surjection A → P(A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard proof uses the diagonal/subset argument: assume surjection f : A → P(A), define B = { x ∈ A : x ∉ f(x) } and derive contradiction by considering whether a ∈ B where f(a)=B. This theorem yields the strict inequality and produces the infinite chain of larger and larger cardinalities via repeated power sets. Students should be able to present the diagonal argument clearly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition 13.4 — Comparison of cardinalities (≤ and <)
rubrics_metrics.description: For sets A,B: |A| = |B| if there is a bijection A → B. |A| < |B| means there is an injection A → B but no surjection A → B. |A| ≤ |B| means |A| < |B| or |A| = |B|.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To show |A| < |B|, exhibit an injection A → B and prove no surjection exists (often by a diagonal argument). To show |A| ≤ |B| it suffices to exhibit an injection A → B (Schröder–Bernstein later gives a converse). Use examples: inclusion N ↪ R shows ℵ0 ≤ |R|; combine with Cantor to get ℵ0 < |R|.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem 13.8 — Infinite subset of a countably infinite set is countably infinite
rubrics_metrics.description: If B is countably infinite and A ⊆ B is infinite, then A is countably infinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: list B as b1,b2,... and select elements that belong to A in order to produce an infinite listing of A. Useful criterion for proving countability of subsets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem 13.9 — Superset of an uncountable set is uncountable
rubrics_metrics.description: If U ⊆ A and U is uncountable, then A is uncountable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by contradiction: if A were countable then any infinite subset U⊆A would be countable (Theorem 13.8), contradiction. Use this to prove sets uncountable by embedding known uncountable sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equality of cardinalities is an equivalence relation
rubrics_metrics.description: The relation '|A| = |B|' (existence of a bijection A → B) is reflexive, symmetric and transitive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reflexive: identity map A→A is a bijection. Symmetric: inverse of bijection is bijection. Transitive: composition of bijections is bijection. This justifies chaining bijections to prove equalities of cardinalities (used in Examples 13.3–13.4).
